descricao: Pesquisa do tambor rotativo em batelada (Beston, UFRJ/IVIG): resultados brutos das frentes R1-R5 e verificacoes concluidas. Sintese escrita a mao em brief_tambor_batelada.md.

sweep:feed.topic: THREAD R2: feed and kinetics for mixed marine and post-consumer litter (Guanabara Bay, UFRJ/IVIG BLJ-16-type batch rotary drum at about 500 °C). Covers feed composition, moisture, sand, salt and bulk density; pyrolysis yields and product properties for marine and mixed post-consumer feeds; kinetics for the missing components (cellulose and paper, wood and biomass, tyre rubber, PVC, EPS, moisture); and a recommended lumped multi-component scheme with char/coke. It builds on brief_forno_rotativo.md §3.5–3.7 and pesquisa_completa.json D_chem, and does not redo the polyolefin RS-L2, PVC, PET or freeboard-cracking items already verified there.

findings.parameter: IVIG/COPPE/UFRJ reactor identity
findings.value: Pyrolysis reactor 'based on technologies used in BLJ-16 type systems, developed by the Chinese company Beston Group'. It processes residual biomass and plastic waste into condensable vapours (oil), combustible gases and biochar. The non-condensable gas is 'reused as a source of thermal energy for the process itself'. The gas is described as 'composed mainly of hydrogen, carbon monoxide, methane, and other light hydrocarbons'. The page also lists 'Sodium Carbonate' as a separate item.
findings.context: Institutional page for the reactor in the professor's video. Confirms the furnace is fired with recycled pyrolysis gas. My inference, not stated on the page: the sodium carbonate item suggests an alkaline additive or scrubber for HCl and acids.
findings.source: IVIG/COPPE/UFRJ, 'Pirólise' web page (English version)
findings.evidence: Page text read via curl. The linked 'Document.pdf' files are Wix links and were not retrieved.

findings.parameter: IVIG pyrolysis laboratory (LDP) and the 'Orla Sem Lixo' project
findings.value: LDP (Laboratório de Pesquisa Aplicada em Descarbonização e Pirólise de Resíduos) opened 10 Dec 2025 on Ilha do Fundão with R$ 7 million of FAPERJ funding. Earlier, the 2022 UFRJ 'Orla Sem Lixo' project (coordinator Susana Vinzón) targeted floating litter at Fundão for chemical recycling by pyrolysis. Agência Brasil, citing Abrelpe: more than 90 t/d of waste, mostly plastic, enters Guanabara Bay.
findings.context: Background for the feed. The material is floating and coastal litter from around Fundão and Guanabara.
findings.source: IVIG news page / Agência Brasil 2022 'UFRJ busca solução sustentável para lixo flutuante no Fundão'
findings.evidence: Search-engine extraction. A direct curl of the article returned no matching text.

findings.parameter: Beston BLJ-16 family (vendor)
findings.value: Batch, 1 batch/day. BLJ-16 WAX and BLJ-16 CAT take waste-plastic bales (max 0.9×0.9×1.6 m) at 8–10 t/batch. BLJ-16 Standard takes whole or sidewall-removed tyres at 15–16 t/batch. BLJ-16 TDU takes oil soil at 16–18 t/batch. Reactor material: Q345R boiler steel (Standard, 2–3 years life) or 304 SS (5–8 years). BLJ-20 reactor is ø2800×10000 mm. Separately, Beston test reports give oil yields of HDPE >85%, LDPE ~80%, PP ~70% and mixed bottle-cap plastic 80% ('reference only').
findings.context: Industrial BLJ-16 is far larger than the ~1 m-door unit in the IVIG video; IVIG says 'based on' BLJ-16 technology. Use the industrial values for scale and the vendor yields only as an upper bound for clean single polymers.
findings.source: Beston Group, 'Pyrolysis Plant for Sale' parameter table and 'Plastic pyrolysis to oil product test reports'
findings.evidence: Parameter table parsed cell by cell from the vendor page. Yield sentence read on bestongroup.com/test-reports/plastic-pyrolysis-to-oil-product-test-reports/amp/

findings.parameter: Guanabara Bay beach litter composition (item counts)
findings.value: 1999–2008, six beaches on the eastern margin, 21,841 items (14,505 summer / 7,336 winter). Plastic 70.6%, construction material 10%, glass 8.1%, EPS (isopor) 7.0%, paper 6.7%, cans 4.8%, modified wood 4.6%, textiles 3.6%, misc. metals 3.2%, footwear 1.6%.
findings.context: The only Guanabara composition with numbers I found. It is a count, the listed shares sum to about 120% (overlapping categories or a typo in the abstract), and it covers beach-stranded, not floating, litter. Use it qualitatively: plastic dominates and EPS, paper, wood, textiles and rubber footwear are present.
findings.source: Baptista Neto J.A., Fonseca E.M. (2011) Variação sazonal, espacial e composicional de lixo ao longo das praias da margem oriental da Baía de Guanabara (1999-2008). Rev. Gestão Costeira Integrada 11(1):31-39, doi:10.5894/rgci189
findings.evidence: Abstract (PT) read on the journal page

findings.value: 138 kg of rejects. Plastic 47.78% (rigid 32.52, film 15.26), fine aggregate (sand/grit) 10.55, paper 6.05, cardboard 5.61. Potentially recyclable 75.64%, contaminants 24.36%. Plastics only: PS 29.77, unidentified 24.08, PET 13.16, PP 11.88, LDPE 9.06, others/multimaterial 5.06, PVC 3.60, HDPE 2.25, degraded/dirty adhered 1.15. Per-cooperative spread: PS 18.8–37.0, PET 10.5–17.1, PP 8.8–18.0, LDPE 2.9–9.1, HDPE 1.6–5.4, PVC 2.5–8.1.

findings.parameter: Guanabara interception system and litter flux
findings.value: 17 ecobarriers and 10 ecoboats were installed in Guanabara Bay before the 2016 Olympics (Fries et al. 2019). They intercepted a significant amount but did not solve the problem. Press figures: ecobarriers captured 4,246 t in 2012, and about 90 t/d of litter enters via rivers and canals. Canal do Cunha carries about 50% of the floating litter (FAPESP).
findings.context: Feed availability and origin. No published mass composition of ecobarrier or ecoboat catch for Guanabara was found.
findings.source: Elliff C.I. et al. (2025) Assessment of marine litter barrier initiatives and their potential as a prevention strategy in Brazil. Ocean Coast. Res., doi:10.1590/2675-2824073.23167; press via search
findings.evidence: USP PDF read for the 17/10 count. The tonnages come from search snippets of O Globo, Oeco and FAPESP (secondary).

findings.parameter: Other Brazilian litter compositions (spread)
findings.value: Ecobarriers in Avaré/Itaí/Arandu (SP), 2024-25: plastic 36.80%, rejects 33.78%, organic 29.42% (by weight). Subtidal benthic litter off Rio: plastic 55.08%, metals 14.97%, fishing gear 12.48%. Microplastics at Jurujuba (Guanabara): HDPE 38%, PP 21%, styrene 10% of polymers.
findings.context: Shows that river-barrier catch can carry about 30% organics (vegetation). Expect wood, leaves and coconut husk in Guanabara floating litter.
findings.source: Search-engine extractions of a redalyc paper (SP ecobarriers), USP OCR 224027 (benthic Rio), and the 2020 Niterói microplastic study
findings.evidence: Snippets only

findings.parameter: Marine-litter batch pyrolysis, unsorted (Venice Lagoon/N. Adriatic, marGnet): mass balance
findings.value: Oil (RPO) 45 wt%, non-condensed gas 26 wt%, solid residue 26 wt% (net of additive). Batch 100 L stirred/cylindrical reactor, ID 320 mm, wall 400 ± 50 °C, autogenic pressure, 15 kW electric. 14 cycles of 4–11.5 kg dry litter (100 kg total), 4 h per cycle, plus 1 kg CaO-based additive per cycle (CaO > 57%, CaO+MgO > 92%) against HCl and organic acids.
findings.context: The best direct analogue for unsorted marine litter. Feed: two-thirds general containers (hard boxes, films, bottles, PP mussel nets, boat parts) and one-third fishing nets (PA6/6.6 and PE), plus some floating styrofoam. Contaminants: seaweed, mussel residue and sand. Tyres were excluded.
findings.source: Faussone G.C., Cecchi T. (2022) Chemical Recycling of Plastic Marine Litter... Sustainability 14:1235, §2.1-2.2
findings.evidence: 'Mass balance was 45 wt% RPO (ml-py), 26 wt% noncondensed gas, and 26 wt% solid residues (net of additive)'; 'Each pyrolysis cycle lasted 4 h'

findings.parameter: Marine-litter raw pyrolysis oil: distillation split
findings.value: Simple distillation of the raw oil gave 23 vol% virgin naphtha (<180 °C cut), 52 vol% marine gasoil (180–320 °C), 6 vol% residue (>320 °C), 10 vol% water and 9 vol% loss as gas. The main marker is 2,4-dimethyl-1-heptene (PP), 16.51% area in the naphtha. The naphtha is rich in BTX, ethylbenzene, styrene and alpha-olefins. Naphthalenes are attributed to PVC/LDPE.
findings.context: Use for the boiling-cut lumps (O light vs W heavy) and for the water carried with the 'oil' from wet, organic-contaminated litter.
findings.source: Faussone & Cecchi 2022, §2.3 and §3
findings.evidence: '23 vol% VN (ml-py), 52 vol% MGO (ml-py), 6 vol% residue, 10 vol% water, and 9 vol% loss'

findings.parameter: Marine-litter gasoil (180–320 °C cut) properties
findings.value: Kinematic viscosity 1.848 mm2/s at 50 °C; density 802.9 kg/m3 at 15 °C; cetane index 61.3; D86 10/50/90% at 178.3/257.1/347.0 °C; S 196 ppm; flash point 58.0 °C; pour point −6 °C; cloud point 14 °C; acid value 0.136 mg KOH/g; carbon residue <0.10%; ash <0.001%; water 0.01 vol%.
findings.context: Properties of the distilled middle cut, not of the raw dark oil shown in the video. The raw oil is heavier and waxy.
findings.source: Faussone & Cecchi 2022, Table 1
findings.evidence: Table 1 read

findings.parameter: Real post-consumer plastic waste (Basque MSW sorting rejects): composition, bulk density and analysis
findings.value: FILM sample, raw: polyolefins 75.0, styrenics 1.7, PVC 4.5, PET 3.4, multimaterial 3.4, other organic 0.8, inorganic 5.4, celluloses 5.5, textile 0.2 wt%; bulk density 0.093; Cl 4.1 wt%; HHV 36.3 MJ/kg; moisture/VM/FC/ash 0.7/91.1/1.6/6.6. PAPER-rich raw: polyolefins 36.1, styrenics 8.8, PVC 2.8, PET 5.3, inorganic 13.4, celluloses 31.5; bulk density 0.253; Cl 1.6; HHV 22.8; moisture/VM/FC/ash 3.5/77.9/7.0/11.6. After flotation pre-treatment, the film sample was 93.1% polyolefins, 0% PVC, Cl 0.2%.
findings.units: wt%; bulk density as printed (header says kg m-3, but the values are evidently g cm-3, i.e. 93 and 253 kg/m3); MJ/kg
findings.context: The closest fully tabulated 'mixed post-consumer' feed. Note how little PVC (4.5%) gives 4.1% Cl, so other chlorinated items or salts may contribute.
findings.source: Fulgencio-Medrano L. et al. (2022) Oil Production by Pyrolysis of Real Plastic Waste. Polymers 14:553, Tables 2-4
findings.evidence: Tables 2, 3 and 4 read

findings.parameter: Real post-consumer plastic waste: yields at 460 °C (semi-batch, 15 °C/min, N2 80 mL/min)
findings.value: Film raw: organic oil 61.0, aqueous 0.0, gas 14.3 (by difference), solid 24.7. Film pre-treated: 70.6 / 0 / 12.8 / 16.6. Paper-rich raw: 17.8 / 19.9 / 21.7 / 40.6. Paper pre-treated: 42.5 / 10.9 / 20.0 / 26.6. WEEE raw: 51.6 / 0 / 19.9 / 28.5. Oil yield rises from 460 to 490 °C. Lopez et al. got 65 wt% liquid at 500 °C with 92.3% plastic feed. PE-rich samples give a waxy product that clogs condensers.
findings.context: The 'about 70% oil' claimed in the video is reached only by a sorted, polyolefin-rich, dry feed. Raw mixed feed gives about 45–61%, and cellulose drives the aqueous phase and char.
findings.source: Fulgencio-Medrano et al. 2022, Table 6 and text
findings.evidence: Table 6 read; 'Lopez et al. obtained 65 wt.% of liquid yield at 500 °C using a sample that contained 92.3 wt.% of plastic'

findings.parameter: Real post-consumer plastic waste: oil HHV and halogen transfer
findings.value: HHV of the organic oil: film raw 40.4, PT-film 42.6, paper 37.4, PT-paper 39.2, WEEE 39.7 MJ/kg. Cl in oil: film raw 12,213 ppm (30% of feed Cl transferred to the oil), PT-film 160 ppm (8%), paper 1479 ppm (9%), PT-paper 894 (10%), WEEE 13,078 (30%). At 490 °C the PT-film oil reached 44.3 MJ/kg with 128 ppm Cl and 65% paraffinic area.
findings.context: Without additive, 8–30% of feed chlorine ends up in the oil as organochlorines. The rest goes to HCl gas, the aqueous phase or the char.
findings.source: Fulgencio-Medrano et al. 2022, Table 7 and abstract
findings.evidence: Table 7 read

findings.parameter: Chlorine partition: pure PVC and PVC with biomass
findings.value: Pure PVC: 96.9 wt% of Cl to gas, 2.9% to oil, 0.04% to char (Ephraim et al., cited). Wood + plastics co-pyrolysis: the apparent drop in HCl yield is mainly HCl dissolving in the water of the condensed oil, not formation of organochlorines. Biomass + PVC at 873 K: more PVC shifts Cl predominantly into the oil phase (Jerzak & Magdziarz 2025). Pre-treating PVC at 593 K removes 99% of its Cl.
findings.context: With wet marine litter, expect HCl to end up in the aqueous condensate, making it corrosive. The CaO (Faussone) or Na2CO3 (IVIG page) additive captures it in the char.
findings.source: Sciforum manuscript citing Ephraim et al.; HAL hal-01802140 (Mines Albi, co-pyrolysis of wood and plastics); Jerzak & Magdziarz, Thermochim. Acta 2025 (AGH repository)
findings.evidence: Search snippets only. HAL is behind an Anubis challenge and the Sciforum PDF returned HTML; neither was bypassed.

findings.parameter: Cellulose kinetics: two parallel extended Prout–Tompkins reactions (microgranular cellulose)
findings.value: dx/dt = −A exp(−E/RT) x^n (1−0.99x)^m. Reaction 1: f1 = 0.75, A1 = 1.94e15 s-1, E1 = 202.65 kJ/mol, n1 = 1, m1 = 0.481. Reaction 2: f2 = 0.163, A2 = 1.63e20 s-1, E2 = 255 kJ/mol, n2 = 22, m2 = 1 (fixed), the slow residual step above about 350 °C. Single first-order alternative (Várhegyi): E = 238 ± 10 kJ/mol, A = 5e17–2e18 s-1. Other fits: Burnham & Braun A = 2.57e14 s-1, E = 196.33 kJ/mol; Whatman CF11 A = 1.4e14 s-1, E = 197 kJ/mol, m = 0.38. Literature E spans 100–250, mostly 190–250 kJ/mol.
findings.context: For the paper/cardboard lump. Pure cellulose leaves only 12.5–17.3% char (Table 2, depending on sample mass). Paper in a kiln gives 30–40% solid because of fillers and ash (11.6% ash in the Basque paper sample).
findings.source: Capart R., Khezami L., Burnham A.K. (2004) Assessment of various kinetic models for the pyrolysis of a microgranular cellulose. Thermochim. Acta 417:79-89 (LLNL UCRL-JRNL-201926)

findings.parameter: Wood/biomass kinetics: Shafizadeh–Chin three parallel primary reactions plus secondary tar reactions
findings.context: For wood, pruning, coconut husk and seaweed in the litter. With the oak set, the primary split at 500 °C is gas/tar/char 0.09/0.62/0.29, and 0.14/0.56/0.30 at 400 °C (derived here).
findings.source: Navarrete Cereijo G., Galione Klot P., Curto-Risso P. (2024) Two-Stage Global Biomass Pyrolysis Model for Combustion Applications. Energies 17:4982, Table 2
findings.evidence: Table 2 read. The primary references (Shafizadeh & Chin 1977; Di Blasi 1993) were not read.

findings.parameter: Heat of biomass pyrolysis (sign depends on char yield)
findings.value: Primary reactions are mostly endothermic (tar formation) and secondary or char-forming reactions exothermic. With the Milosavljevic correlation the enthalpy ranges from −313 to +526 kJ/kg; Park's correlation gives −25.2 to +53.7 kJ/kg. The reaction turns exothermic when char exceeds about 20%, which occurs below 670 K. Tar HHV 20–26 MJ/kg; char HHV 30–35 MJ/kg.
findings.context: For the energy equation of the cellulosic lump: use a small net endotherm and test −300 to +500 kJ/kg as a sensitivity.
findings.source: Navarrete Cereijo et al. 2024, §1 (citing Milosavljevic et al. 1996, Park et al. 2010, Rath et al. 2003)
findings.evidence: 'The enthalpy range varies between −313 and 526 kJ/kg using the correlation proposed by Milosavljevic ... between −25.2 and 53.7 kJ/kg according to ... Park'

findings.parameter: Tyre/rubber kinetics: three independent first-order components
findings.value: Fractions of total mass loss: 'oil etc.' (oils, plasticisers, additives) z1 = 0.0528, NR z2 = 0.294, SBR/BR z3 = 0.653. Fit (10 K/min): oil etc. A = 3.8e2 min-1, E = 33.1 kJ/mol; NR 3.1e9 min-1, 124.1; SBR/BR 1.6e11 min-1, 161.6. Literature spread: Leung & Wang 1999 oil 2.0e4/52.5, NR 6.3e13/164.5, SBR 2.3e9/136.1; Mui 2010 NR 1.9e7/102.8, SBR 1.13e17/237.1; Kim 1995 NR 3.78e16/209.0, SBR 8.75e8/127.3; González 2001 values are much lower. Typical tyre char 38–40 wt% (Williams 2013).
findings.context: For tyres, rubber footwear and rubber debris. The mantissa/exponent split was reconstructed from a pdftotext string with flattened superscripts (e.g. '3.1109' read as 3.1×10^9), so check against the PDF before coding.
findings.source: Cherbański R., Wróblewski K., Molga E. (2017) Pyrolysis of waste tyres – the effect of reaction kinetics on the results of thermogravimetric analysis. Chem. Process Eng. 38(3):363-377, Table 2
findings.evidence: Table 2 and the z_i sentence read. Exponent reconstruction needs checking against the PDF.

findings.parameter: Tyre pyrolysis yields and energy (from previous round, re-used)
findings.value: Pilot continuous kiln: char about 39.8 wt% (roughly constant over 450–650 °C), oil max 45.1 wt% at 500 °C, oil HHV 40–42 MJ/kg. Gamboa 2023: heat demand 1.41–2.16 kJ/g at 698–848 K; 30–50% of the gas covers it; gas LHV 37.3 MJ/kg.
findings.context: Product split for the rubber lump.
findings.source: pesquisa_completa.json (A_designs; H_static verdicts): Li S.Q. et al. 2004; Gamboa et al. Energies 16 (2023) 7932
findings.evidence: Carried over from earlier verification rounds

findings.parameter: Activation-temperature staging at slow (batch) heating (derived)
findings.value: Temperature at which k = 1e-3 s-1 (time scale about 17 min): PVC stage I 251 °C; cellulose about 300–306 °C; Shafizadeh–Chin oak tar 339 °C; tyre NR 332 °C (Cherbański) or 299 °C (Leung); PS 370 °C; PET 395 °C; PVC stage II 397 °C; SBR 399–406 °C; PP 402 °C; LDPE 417 °C; HDPE 429 °C. At 500 °C, k is 0.04–0.06 s-1 for the polyolefins (RS-L2), 0.17 for PET, 0.28 for PS and 0.1 for oak tar.
findings.context: In a 6–8 h batch the products come off in sequence: water (100 °C), then HCl (250–330 °C), then biomass vapours, water, CO and CO2, then styrene, then polyolefin oil and wax. This sequence is the time series for the live plot.
findings.source: Derived here (scratchpad r2calc/k.py) from the parameter sets above and the RS-L2/PVC/PET sets in the brief
findings.evidence: Arrhenius evaluation. The P2, F3, n = 22 and Prout–Tompkins rate laws make the single-k comparison approximate.

findings.parameter: PVC two-stage kinetics and Cl stoichiometry (already verified; restated for the lumped scheme)
findings.value: Stage I (P2): 75 kJ/mol, A 1.81e6 min-1 (3.0e4 s-1), releases 0.583 kg HCl per kg PVC. Stage II (F3): 140 kJ/mol, A 4.84e9 min-1 (8.07e7 s-1). PVC fixed carbon 5.2–6.3 wt%. Cl mass fraction is 0.567 in PVC and 0.607 in NaCl (stoichiometry).
findings.context: Re-used from brief §3.6 [41]. The heat of PVC dehydrochlorination was again not found in any source this round.
findings.source: Polymers 2021 PMC8706959 (via brief)
findings.evidence: From the earlier full-text verification

findings.parameter: Feed moisture, ash and bulk-density envelope
findings.value: Hamm ConTherm RDF feed: moisture 5–50 wt%, ash 3–23 wt%, bulk density 60–250 kg/m3, LHV 11–28 MJ/kg, Cl 0.1–3.0 wt% (previous round, full text). Beston screw feed for plastics requires moisture <10% and pieces ≤5 cm (vendor). Basque raw film/paper samples: moisture 0.7/3.5%, ash 6.6/11.6%, bulk density about 93/253 kg/m3. Rio cooperative rejects: fine aggregate 10.55%.
findings.context: No measured moisture or salt content for collected Guanabara litter was found. As-collected marine litter is wet; the base case assumes 10–20% moisture after drainage and sun-drying, with 30% as a stress case.
findings.source: DGEngineering Hamm sheet (2009); Beston FAQ; Fulgencio-Medrano 2022; Cruz 2024
findings.evidence: Combination of full-text values (Hamm, Fulgencio, Cruz) and vendor values (Beston)

findings.parameter: Mixed-plastic and MSW rotary-kiln yields at about 500 °C (previous round, re-used as validation spread)
findings.value: Bhatt 2026 semi-pilot kiln, 500 °C: mixed plastics 43 wt% oil, 16 wt% char. Wastepaper 30–40 wt% char. Mixed MSW in the literature: 38–56% liquid, 17–25% char. Chinese commercial kilns: oil 43–52%, carbon black 30–40%, gas 6–25%. ASR bench kiln gas LHV 18–26 MJ/Nm3 (dry).
findings.context: Together with Faussone (45/26/26) and Fulgencio (61/14/25 raw film), this brackets the IVIG claim of about 70% oil.
findings.source: pesquisa_completa.json D_chem and A_designs (Bhatt et al. RSC Adv. 2026 PMC12927709; Ma & Zhong 2018; Notarnicola 2017)
findings.evidence: Carried over from the earlier round

findings.parameter: Pyrolysis gas heating value (spread)
findings.value: LDPE/HDPE semi-batch gas: LHV 47.03–49.99 MJ/kg (Ejeh 2016, Aspen-calculated). Tyre pyrolysis gas: LHV 37.3 MJ/kg (Gamboa 2023); batch tyre plant GCV about 37 MJ/m3 (methane, ethane, butadiene). ASR kiln: 18–26 MJ/Nm3, rising with temperature. IVIG describes its gas as H2, CO, CH4 and light hydrocarbons.

findings.parameter: Marine fishing-net and fish-bag pyrolysis (spread)
findings.value: PE/PP fish-feed bags (Memorial Univ.): maximum wax/oil 69–75 wt% at 500 °C, residue 6–7%, gas 23–25%. SEAFDEC (Thailand) marine debris at 400–550 °C: oil recovery 47.3% from plastic bags versus 20.0% from nylon netting fragments.

findings.parameter: Base-case lumped feed and derived yields (assumed composition)
findings.value: Dry basis: PE 40, PP 20, PS/EPS 12, PET 6, PVC 2, rubber 3, cellulosic (paper, wood, organics) 8, inorganic (sand, salt, grit) 9 wt%. Using the per-component splits in the notes, the derived dry-basis yields are organic oil+wax 68.3, aqueous 1.9, gas 13.4, HCl 1.2, char+ash 15.3 wt%. As received with 10/20/30% moisture: oil 61.5/54.6/47.8, aqueous 11.7/21.5/31.3, gas 12.1/10.7/9.4, char 13.7/12.2/10.7 wt%.

findings.source: Derived here (scratchpad r2calc/k.py); split anchors from Faussone 2022, Fulgencio-Medrano 2022, Capart 2004, Cherbański 2017 and the brief

findings.parameter: Salt chlorine from seawater-wet litter (assumed inputs)
findings.value: If 20% of the wet mass is retained brackish water at 30 g/kg salinity, NaCl is about 0.6 wt% wet, or 0.75 wt% dry, which carries about 0.45 wt% Cl. For comparison, 2% PVC carries 1.13 wt% Cl. NaCl stays in the char/ash at 500 °C because it melts at 801 °C.
findings.context: Salt adds roughly 40% on top of the PVC chlorine but goes to the char, not to the HCl gas. Do not route it through the HCl lump.
findings.source: Derived here from stoichiometry and assumed salinity/retention
findings.evidence: Stoichiometric calculation. Salinity and water retention are assumptions; no measured salt content of the litter was found.

equations.name: Cellulose: extended Prout–Tompkins, two parallel reactions
equations.variables: x_i = unreacted fraction of reaction i (starts at 1); f_i = mass fraction volatilised by reaction i; residue 1 - f1 - f2 ≈ 0.087 for pure cellulose at TGA scale (measured char 12.5–17%)
equations.validity: Microgranular cellulose, TGA, 1–11 K/min, isothermal and dynamic data. The (1 - 0.99x) term needs x starting at 1 (no seed required).
equations.source: Capart, Khezami, Burnham 2004, Thermochim. Acta 417:79 (LLNL UCRL-JRNL-201926), Eq. 11 and §4

equations.name: Wood/biomass: Shafizadeh–Chin with secondary tar reactions
equations.expression: dm_B/dt = -(k_G + k_T + k_C) m_B;  dm_T/dt = k_T m_B - (k_TG + k_TC) m_T;  dm_G/dt = k_G m_B + k_TG m_T;  dm_C/dt = k_C m_B + k_TC m_T;  k = A exp(-E/RT)
equations.validity: Wood particles, about 300–600 °C. Tar secondary reactions apply in hot pores and in the freeboard gas.
equations.source: Navarrete Cereijo et al. 2024, Energies 17:4982, Table 2 and Eq. 33

equations.name: Tyre rubber: independent parallel first-order components
equations.expression: dα_i/dt = A_i exp(-E_i/RT)(1 - α_i);  volatile fraction = Σ_i z_i α_i,  i ∈ {oil etc., NR, SBR/BR}
equations.variables: z = 0.0528 / 0.294 / 0.653. A = 3.8e2 / 3.1e9 / 1.6e11 min-1. E = 33.1 / 124.1 / 161.6 kJ/mol. The non-volatile remainder (carbon black + ash, about 0.38–0.40 of the tyre) is inert char.
equations.validity: TGA of end-of-life tyre, 10 K/min, 400–1000 K
equations.source: Cherbański, Wróblewski, Molga 2017, Chem. Process Eng. 38:363, Eqs. 1-4 and Table 2

equations.name: Moisture evaporation (heat-sink / boiling-plateau model)
equations.expression: if T_cell >= T_b and m_w > 0:  ṁ_evap = q_net / h_fg  (T clamped at T_b);  else ṁ_evap = 0;  T_b = 100 °C, h_fg = 2257 kJ/kg
equations.variables: q_net = net heat into the cell (W); m_w = water mass in the cell
equations.validity: Bulk bed with slow heating (hours). An Arrhenius drying form (A about 5.13e10 s-1, E about 88 kJ/mol, attributed to Chan et al. 1985) is widely used in particle models but was not verified this session.
equations.source: Standard enthalpy method [H]; h_fg from the steam tables

equations.name: Additive product yields of a multi-component feed
equations.expression: Y_j = Σ_i w_i y_ij,  j ∈ {O, W, A, OX, H2O, G, HCl, CHAR, ASH}
equations.variables: w_i = dry mass fraction of component i; y_ij = mass yield of lump j from component i (table in notes)
equations.validity: Westerhout showed additivity for LDPE/PP at 425 °C (brief). Interactions exist for PVC with PE/biomass (Cl shifts to oil/aqueous) and PET with PE (sublimates, wax). Treat these as corrections.
equations.source: Brief §3.6 [33]; this report

equations.name: Chlorine balance
equations.expression: Cl_feed = 0.567 w_PVC + 0.607 w_NaCl + Cl_other;  Y_HCl,max = 0.583 w_PVC;  Cl_oil ≈ (0.08–0.30) Cl_feed without additive
equations.variables: w = dry mass fractions
equations.validity: Stoichiometry. The fraction of Cl to the oil is from Fulgencio-Medrano 2022, Table 7 (semi-batch, 460–490 °C).
equations.source: Stoichiometry; Fulgencio-Medrano et al. 2022

sweep:feed.notes:
WHAT IS NEW VERSUS THE BRIEF. The brief (§3.6) covered polyolefins (RS-L2/Westerhout), PVC (two-stage), PET (first order) and paper (char 0.3–0.4 only). This round adds the following, read in full text:
(a) a real marine-litter batch benchmark (Faussone 2022);
(b) a real mixed post-consumer feed with Cl and aqueous phase (Fulgencio-Medrano 2022);
(c) a Rio-specific gravimetric polymer split (Cruz 2024, UFRRJ);
(d) cellulose kinetics (Capart/Burnham, LLNL);
(e) wood Shafizadeh–Chin sets with secondary tar reactions and enthalpy spreads (Navarrete 2024);
(f) three-component tyre kinetics (Cherbański 2017);
(g) confirmation that IVIG's reactor is a Beston BLJ-16-type batch unit whose pyrolysis gas heats the process.

GAPS (stated honestly).
- No published MASS composition of Guanabara floating/ecobarrier catch was found. Only beach item counts (2011) and Rio cooperative rejects (2024) exist; INEA reports were not found.
- No measured moisture or salt content of collected Guanabara litter.
- No open source for the heat of PVC dehydrochlorination; keep 0.3–0.5 MJ/kg as [H, unverified].
- The Chan 1985 moisture Arrhenius constants were not verified.
- Nylon (PA6/6.6) net kinetics were not gathered. PA appears as about one-third of Faussone's marine plastics, and nylon nets gave only 20% oil (SEAFDEC, snippet).
- No gas composition (vol%) for mixed marine litter at 500 °C; only LHV spreads.
- Blocked without bypass: SciELO (Bunny Shield), addi.ehu.eus (reCAPTCHA), HAL Mines-Albi (Anubis), Sciforum. The Semantic Scholar API returned 429.

RECOMMENDED LUMPED SCHEME for the batch drum at about 500 °C (bed = pseudo-components; products = lumps O light oil C5–C20, W wax C21+, A aromatics/styrene-rich, OX oxygenates/sublimates, H2O, G non-condensable gas, HCl, CHAR, ASH). Yields are per kg of component.

1. H2O (free moisture), base 10–20% wet, stress 30%. Boiling-plateau model at 100 °C, h_fg 2257 kJ/kg. Goes to H2O vapour, which condenses into the aqueous phase of the 'oil'.

2. Polyolefins.
- LDPE/HDPE (films, bags, bottles, PE nets) and PP (caps, mussel nets, laminates): existing RS-L2 sets (HDPE 238/5.2e14, LDPE 215/1.92e13, PP 179/6.98e10).
- PE yields: G 0.10, O 0.55, W 0.34, CHAR 0.01.
- PP yields: G 0.12, O 0.60, W 0.26, CHAR 0.02.
- Char values follow the fixed carbon of 0–1.2% (brief).
- ΔH: PE 0.92, PP 1.31 MJ/kg; melting 218/80 J/g.

3. PS and EPS (food boxes, cups, foam). Use the RS-L2 PS set (180/4.1e11).
- Yields: A 0.65 (styrene-rich), O 0.25, G 0.05, CHAR 0.05 [S/H].
- ΔH 1.0 MJ/kg.
- EPS enters at about 10–30 kg/m3 bulk [H], so it dominates the charge volume, not the mass.

4. PET (bottles, polyester textiles). First order, 210 kJ/mol, 2.59e13 s-1.
- Yields: CHAR 0.15 (0.10–0.20), OX 0.40 (benzoic/terephthalic acid sublimates and acetaldehyde, which foul condensers), G 0.43 (CO, CO2), H2O 0.02 [H].
- ΔH 0.3–0.5 MJ/kg [unverified].

5. PVC (pipes, cables, toys).
- Stage I (P2): 75 kJ/mol, 3.0e4 s-1, seed α0 1e-4. Releases HCl 0.583 kg/kg PVC, of which about 97% goes to gas.
- Stage II (F3): 140 kJ/mol, 8.07e7 s-1, acting on the polyene residue (0.417). Products: A (benzene/naphthalenes) about 0.25, G about 0.06 and CHAR about 0.10 per kg of PVC (fixed carbon 5.2–6.3% gives the lower bound) [H].
- Interactions: HCl dissolves in the condensed water. With PE and biomass, 8–30% of the Cl leaves in the oil as organochlorines (Fulgencio Table 7). CaO or Na2CO3 in the charge converts HCl to CaCl2/NaCl in the char (Faussone used 1 kg CaO-based additive per 4–11.5 kg).

6. CELL lump (paper, cardboard, wood, coconut husk, seaweed, leaves).
- Paper: Capart two-reaction cellulose model.
- Wood/husk: Shafizadeh–Chin (oak) with tar→gas and tar→char.
- Yields at 500 °C, per kg of dry ash-free cellulosic: CHAR 0.25–0.30, OX (organic) 0.15–0.20, reaction H2O 0.20, G 0.25–0.30 (CO, CO2, CH4, H2). Check against Fulgencio raw paper: 17.8 org / 19.9 aq / 21.7 gas / 40.6 solid with 13.4% inorganic.
- ΔH from −0.3 to +0.5 MJ/kg depending on char.
- Paper filler/ash (about 10–12%) goes to ASH.

7. RUB (tyres, footwear, rubber debris). Cherbański three-component model.
- Yields: O 0.40, A 0.05, G 0.15, CHAR 0.40 (carbon black + ZnO/S ash).
- Total heat demand 1.41–2.16 kJ/g (Gamboa, includes sensible heat).

8. PA (nylon nets). Not covered. Proxy: first order with E about 200 kJ/mol [H]; yields O 0.30, OX/N-compounds 0.40 (caprolactam), G 0.25, CHAR 0.05 [H]. Flag as unverified.

9. INERT. Sand and grit (Rio rejects 10.6% fine aggregate; Fulgencio 5.4–13.4% inorganic), plus NaCl from seawater (about 0.5–1% dry [D/H]). Goes to ASH and stays in the char. NaCl Cl is not HCl.

10. Freeboard, unchanged from brief §3.7. W→O (k_W = 3 k_O), O→G/A with k_O = 1.0e16 exp(−300 kJ/mol/RT). Add OX→G (CO, CO2) as an option, and HCl as an inert tracer.

11. CHAR/COKE. CHAR = Σ char yields + ASH, plus coke from secondary tar→char on the hot wall (k_TC). For the video, report char (carbonised residue) and ash separately.

ASSUMED BASE FEED [H], dry: PE 40, PP 20, PS/EPS 12, PET 6, PVC 2, RUB 3, CELL 8, INERT 9. Bracket it with:
- 'IVIG sorted plastic': PO about 90%, PVC 0;
- 'Rio rejects': PS about 30%, PET 13%, PVC 3.6%, grit 10%.

Derived base-case yields (dry): oil+wax 68, aqueous 2, gas 13, HCl 1.2, char+ash 15 wt%. At 10% moisture as received: 61.5 / 11.7 / 12.1 / 13.7.

VALIDATION LADDER for the feed and chemistry:
- Faussone 45/26/26 (unsorted marine litter, 4 h batch, ±5 points);
- Fulgencio raw film 61/14/25 and sorted 70.6/12.8/16.6 at 460 °C;
- Bhatt mixed plastics 43 oil / 16 char at 500 °C;
- the IVIG claim of about 70% oil (video, secondary; plausible only for a dry, sorted, polyolefin-rich charge, or if water is counted as oil);
- vendor HDPE >85 / LDPE 80 / PP 70% as the upper bound.

LIVE-PLOT SUGGESTION. Plot cumulative mass of each product lump against batch time (0–8 h), with bed temperature on a twin axis. The staged release is a physically grounded story for the video:
- water plateau at 100 °C;
- HCl at 250–330 °C;
- CO2/CO, water and tar from biomass at 300–380 °C;
- styrene from EPS at about 370 °C;
- polyolefin oil and wax at 400–450 °C;
- char growing early from cellulose and PET and staying at the end.
Gas LHV over time (low at first from CO2/H2O, then about 45 MJ/kg) drives the furnace combustion and the need for auxiliary fuel early in the batch.

sweep:reactor.topic: THREAD R1: the real UFRJ/IVIG reactor (a Beston batch rotary drum). Identification, size estimate from the video, Beston datasheets (BLJ-3 skid-mounted, BLJ-16/BLJ-20, BST-J batch), and the recommended CFD reference geometry and batch cycle

findings.parameter: Identity and owner of the reactor in the video
findings.value: Laboratório de Pesquisa Aplicada em Descarbonização e Pirólise de Resíduos (LDP), IVIG/COPPE/UFRJ. It sits in a warehouse in the Cidade Universitária (Ilha do Fundão), near Guanabara Bay, on space lent by UFRJ, and is funded by FAPERJ. The lab inaugurated 10 Dec 2025, with R$ 7 million from FAPERJ (title of the IVIG post). The official IVIG page says the lab has 'a pyrolysis reactor based on technologies used in BLJ-16 type systems, developed by the Chinese company Beston Group'. Products named: pyrolytic oil, combustible gases 'reused for energy generation and heating of the process itself', and biochar. CO2 from the reactor and the biomethane generator exhausts is captured in NaOH, giving Na2CO3.
findings.context: The video's sign reads 'LDP / IVIG / Projeto FAPERJ / UFRJ' (frame f_049); the BESTON logo is on the furnace casing (frames f_026-028). The Beston-BLJ-16 sentence is IVIG's own wording.
findings.source: IVIG/UFRJ, 'Pyrolysis' and 'LDP - Laboratório de Pesquisa Aplicada' pages; Biochar Today 14 Dec 2025; IVIG blog posts of 19 Aug and 24 Sep 2026
findings.evidence: Read in full with curl: 'The IVIG/COPPE/UFRJ laboratory has a pyrolysis reactor based on technologies used in BLJ-16 type systems, developed by the Chinese company Beston Group'. The video matches Beston's BLJ-3 skid-mounted photos and 3D render feature by feature:
- A silver cylindrical casing with the BESTON logo, on a steel skid.
- A front hinged, bolted door with a thick insulated plug: a ceramic-fibre block on steel pins, coated in char.

sweep:reactor.notes:
IDENTIFICATION CONFLICT, to state openly in the event. IVIG's official page says the reactor is 'based on technologies used in BLJ-16 type systems' from Beston. The video, however, shows a much smaller, skid-mounted unit. Its drum mouth ring is about 1.25 m and the clear door about 1.0-1.1 m, measured against a 1.75 m worker. It matches Beston's BLJ-3 skid-mounted unit (φ1.4 × 4.9 m) feature by feature: casing, BESTON logo, front insulated door, rear rotary joint and gear drive, side burner gas trains, foil-wrapped manifold, and a condenser box with yellow tube caps. A BLJ-16 drum (about φ2.8 m) would be taller than a person. My reading: the hardware is a BLJ-3-class drum, and 'BLJ-16 type' describes the technology family. This is an inference; no official dimension or tonnage was found. A BST-J12 (φ1.9 × 4.5 m, Beston's batch biochar drum) is a weaker alternative.

RECOMMENDED CFD REFERENCE ('Caso U', UFRJ):
1. Geometry
   - Horizontal drum, ID 1.40 m × L 4.90 m, no slope.
   - Steel wall 12 mm [H] (Q345R or 304; vendor gives no BLJ-3 thickness; 2.2-2.8 m drums use 16-20 mm).
   - Front: hinged insulated door, 1.0-1.1 m clear.
   - Rear: central vapour off-take through a rotary joint (DN about 150 [H]), leading to the vertical manifold / heavy-oil pot, the horizontal tube condensers, the oil tanks, the water seal, and then the burners or the flare.
2. Internals
   - Vendor-faithful baseline: 2-start helical 'spiral plates', height about 0.10 m, pitch about 1.0-1.2 m [H] (Doing/Huayin practice, full text).
   - 'Aletas' variant for the user: 6 straight longitudinal lifters 0.12 m (≈ D/12) [H], cf. Suzuki 6 × 200 mm in a 1 m drum.
   - Static variant (0 rpm) to show the hot-wall hazard.
3. Rotation: base 0.8 rpm; sweep 0, 0.4, 1, 2 rpm. Fr is about 5e-4 at the base speed (rolling/slumping regime).
4. Furnace
   - Stationary casing lined with ceramic fibre.
   - Combustion chamber in the base under the drum, with two forced-draught dual-fuel burners (LPG/NG/diesel plus NCG). Rating about 465 kW is unverified.
   - Flue gas flows up through the annulus around the drum [H gap 0.15-0.25 m] and exits at the top to the chimney through the smoke tube, spray tower and de-dusting.
5. Charge: 0.5-0.8 t of wet mixed marine litter [H]. Loaded loose to F ≤ 2/3 (5.0 m³), collapsing to F ≈ 0.15-0.3 after melting; the final char/ash bed is a few percent of fill.
6. Cycle for the animation
   - t = 0: loaded and sealed, N2 purge, auxiliary burners on.
   - When the vapour line reaches about 180-250 °C (vendor): oil gas appears; NCG is routed to the burners and the auxiliary fuel is turned down.
   - Wall setpoint about 500 °C (UFRJ). Gas-side reading 280-350 °C (vendor gauge).
   - End of pyrolysis at 6-8 h (UFRJ), when the gas flow drops (vendor criterion: reactor temperature rises while the vapour-drum temperature falls).
   - Then cooling 5-9 h and discharge 1-3 h, compressed in the video.
7. Pressure: +2 to +10 kPa(g), relief at 20 kPa (vendor).

sweep:furnace.topic: THREAD R4: the combustion furnace and heat transfer to the batch rotary drum. Covers (1) the non-condensable pyrolysis gas (NCG) from plastics and mixed waste at about 500 °C, the start-up fuel, and how the gas is reused as fuel; (2) furnace (fire box) design of batch rotary drums and burner capacities; (3) heat transfer from flame and flue gas to the rotating shell (WSGG, convection, refractory re-radiation, shell flux and temperature limits, Q245R/Q345R); (4) flame models that fit the existing flare code (mixture fraction with equilibrium/β-PDF, eddy dissipation, WSGG radiation). Target plant: the UFRJ/IVIG Beston-type batch drum processing marine litter from Guanabara Bay at 500 °C, with a 6-8 h batch and a claimed ~70 % oil.

findings.parameter: NCG composition and heating value, individual recovered plastics at 500 °C (lab)
findings.value: Methane is the main NCG species, above 50 vol% (N2-free), for PE, HIPS, EPS, PP and PVC. It peaks between 40 and 80 min of operation. Ethane is second, reaching up to 30 % in some cases (HIPS, EPS, PET), mainly early in the run. H2, ethylene, methyl-acetylene, CO and propane are present at lower levels. PET gas starts CO-rich and the CO falls with time. Average HHV of the N2-free gas ranges from 41.3 MJ/m3 (PP) to 68.1 MJ/m3 (PVC). Yields at 500 °C: EPS oil 66.0 %; gas from 33.0 % (EPS, 500 °C) to 65.1 % (PVC, 525 °C); PP oil 41.4 % (450 °C) rising to 53.6 % (500 °C). The oil maximum is near 500 °C for all polymers except PET and PVC (475 °C).
findings.context: 40 g of crushed plastic sorted by family from a municipal waste plant. Tube furnace, N2 at 100 mL/min, 20 °C/min, 90 min hold. Gas yields are high because they include losses and the gas is diluted by the N2 sweep; use the composition trend, not the yield, for a large drum.
findings.source: Calero M., Solís R.R., Muñoz-Batista M.J., Pérez A., Blázquez G., Martín-Lara M.A. (2023) Chem. Eng. Sci. 271:118569, Sections 3.1 and 3.5, Fig. 6
findings.evidence: Section 3.5 states 'methane ... represents over 50 % and shows a maximum value between 40 and 80 min'. Concluding paragraph: 'the average HHV of N2-free gas varies between 41.3 MJ m-3 for PP and 68.1 MJ m-3 for PVC'.

findings.parameter: Gross calorific value and properties of plastic pyrolysis gases (500/700/900 °C)
findings.value: PE and PP at 500 °C give the most energetic gases: GCV 86.58 and 81.09 MJ/Nm3. PP at 900 °C converts 66.88 wt% of the feed to gas. PP gas at 500 °C has a high specific heat, 2.94 kJ/(Nm3·K). Part II: PVC gases have an average laminar burning velocity of 178.62 cm/s, about 5 times natural gas. PET gases have an upper flammability limit of 61.46 % on average. No gas has a methane number of 65 or more, so none suits gas engines.
findings.context: 24 gases from PET, PP, PE, PVC, PS and 3 mixtures at 500, 700 and 900 °C. Compared with natural gas and propane. A GCV of 81-87 MJ/Nm3 implies a gas rich in C3-C4 (propane is about 101 MJ/Nm3).

findings.value: Heating fuel per tonne of feed: coal 85-90 kg, natural gas 70-80 m3, diesel 55-65 kg, or LPG 50-55 kg. findings.parameter: Start-up and auxiliary fuel switch in batch rotary plants (literature and vendor)
findings.value: Bangladesh commercial batch rotary tyre plant (2 units, 4.5 t/run, 420 °C, 0.03 bar): liquids burned for the first 3 h, then pyro-gas for the remaining 5 h. Doing 10 t batch: about 300 kg diesel, or 300-400 kg pyrolysis oil, or about 150 m3 CNG, or 100-150 kg LPG, or 700-800 kg wood, or about 500 kg coal per batch; average electrical power about 30 kW. Tyre gas LHV averages 37.3 MJ/kg; burning 30-50 % of the gas covers the reaction heat, and poor insulation can break self-sufficiency.

findings.parameter: Shell material limits Q245R / Q345R
findings.value: Supplier statements: Q245R (carbon steel, yield ≥245 MPa) maximum service temperature ≤425 °C. Q345R (low alloy, yield ≥345 MPa) -20 to 475 °C. The allowable-stress tables are in GB/T 150.2-2024, Appendix C (in force 1 Feb 2025), but the numbers were not obtained. Batch drums use 16-20 mm Q245R/Q345R (Doing, Sihai) at 2-10 kPa working pressure (Beston). A shell at 520-650 °C (bed 500 °C plus 20-150 K wall superheat) is therefore above the code temperature range of both grades. Life is governed by creep sag of a hot, slowly rotating horizontal shell, oxidation/scaling on the fire side, and thermal distortion from flame impingement. Pressure stress is negligible at ≤20 kPa.

equations.name: WSGG total emissivity (Smith et al. 1982 form)
equations.expression: eps_g = sum_{i=0}^{3} a_i(T) [1 - exp(-kappa_i (p_w + p_c) L)] ; a_i(T) = sum_{j=1}^{4} b_{i,j} T^{j-1} (i ≥ 1) ; kappa_0 = 0, a_0 = 1 - sum_{i≥1} a_i ; in RTE form, absorption coefficient of gray gas i = kappa_i (p_w + p_c)
equations.variables: T gas temperature [K]; p_w, p_c partial pressures of H2O and CO2 [atm]; L path length [m]; kappa_i [1/(atm m)]; b_ij from Smith Table (see findings)
equations.validity: 1 atm, 600-2400 K, pL 0.001-10 atm·m. Interpolate in Pw/(Pw+Pc). Soot not included: add kappa_soot = 1232·ρ_soot·T·(1+4.8e-4(T-2000)) or our flare soot model.
equations.source: Smith, Shen, Friedman (1982) J. Heat Transfer 104:602, as reproduced in arXiv 2411.18467 App. A/B; ANSYS Fluent Theory Guide §5.3.8 (WSGG form)

equations.name: Mean beam length
equations.expression: L_m = 3.6 V / A (arbitrary enclosure) ; thin annular jacket of gap δ ≈ infinite slab, L_m ≈ 1.76 δ ; kiln freeboard L_m = 0.95 (D - H)
equations.variables: V gas volume; A bounding area; δ jacket gap; D drum diameter; H bed depth
equations.validity: Optically thin to moderate gases. The 1.76δ slab value is standard textbook practice (not re-read here).
equations.source: arXiv 2411.18467 (3.6V/A); Gorog et al. via prior brief (0.95(D-H))

equations.name: Refractory (or burner-box wall) to drum shell radiation, two gray surfaces
equations.expression: q_rs = sigma (T_r^4 - T_s^4) / (1/eps_r + (A_s/A_r)(1/eps_r - 1) + 1/eps_s - 1) ≈ sigma (T_r^4 - T_s^4)/(1/eps_r + 1/eps_s - 1) for A_s ≈ A_r
equations.variables: T_r refractory, T_s shell [K]; eps_r about 0.8-0.9 (refractory/ceramic fibre); eps_s 0.85-0.9 (oxidised steel)
equations.validity: Transparent gas between the surfaces; for a participating gas use the zone method or DOM/P1 with WSGG
equations.source: Standard enclosure radiation (textbook); numbers in findings derived

equations.name: Gas-to-wall radiative flux (Hottel)
equations.expression: q_gw = sigma ((eps_w + 1)/2) (eps_g(T_g) T_g^4 - alpha_g(T_w) T_w^4)
equations.variables: eps_g from WSGG at T_g; alpha_g ≈ eps_g evaluated at T_w (gray approximation); eps_w wall emissivity
equations.validity: eps_w > 0.8; error < 20 % for gray treatment (prior brief)
equations.source: Standard (Hottel); prior brief §3.4

equations.name: Cross-flow convection over the drum (Churchill-Bernstein)
equations.variables: Re = ρ V D/μ with D the drum OD; properties at film temperature
equations.validity: Re·Pr > 0.2, all Re; isolated cylinder (furnace confinement raises h). Standard correlation (Churchill & Bernstein 1977, J. Heat Transfer 99:300), not re-read here.
equations.source: Churchill & Bernstein (1977), textbook

equations.name: Annular jacket forced convection (Gnielinski)
equations.expression: Nu_Dh = (f/8)(Re - 1000) Pr / [1 + 12.7 (f/8)^{1/2} (Pr^{2/3} - 1)], f = (0.79 ln Re - 1.64)^{-2}; laminar annulus Nu ≈ 5 (order of magnitude)
equations.variables: D_h = 2δ for an annulus of gap δ; Re based on D_h
equations.validity: 3000 < Re < 5e6. Standard correlation, not re-read here. In the drum jacket, Re ≈ 2400-2500, so convection is a minor path.
equations.source: Gnielinski (1976), textbook

equations.name: Furnace energy balance (reduced model)
equations.expression: Q_drum = m_f LHV - m_fg c_p,fg (T_out - T_0) - Q_casing ; m_fg = m_f (1 + λ AFR_st) ; T_ad from equilibrium (Cantera) ; Q_casing = sum A_c (T_ci - T_amb)/(δ_ins/k_ins + 1/h_out)
equations.variables: m_f fuel rate; λ excess-air ratio; AFR_st 15.4 (case A) or 9.8 (case B) kg/kg; T_out flue exit; k_ins ceramic fibre about 0.08-0.15 W/mK
equations.validity: Lumped. Validate against 45-65 % efficiency [D] and Hamm/Chalmers loss splits
equations.source: Derived; Hamm sheet; Qasim et al. 2025

equations.name: Mixture fraction for a multi-stream burner (flare code reuse)
equations.expression: Z = (s Y_F - Y_O2 + Y_O2,ox)/(s Y_F,fuel + Y_O2,ox) (Burke-Schumann/Bilger form) ; Z_st = 1/(1 + AFR_st) = 0.061 (case A), 0.092 (case B) ; mean properties = ∫ φ_eq(Z) β(Z; Z̃, Z''²) dZ
equations.variables: s stoichiometric O2/fuel mass ratio; φ_eq equilibrium state (T, ρ, Y_CO2, Y_H2O, soot proxy) from Cantera tables
equations.validity: Fast chemistry. Fuel composition drifts over the batch (start-up diesel/LPG → CO/CO2-rich early NCG → hydrocarbon-rich NCG), so build 3-4 tables and blend by a 'fuel index' or a second mixture fraction for the auxiliary fuel
equations.source: Existing flarekit approach; Z_st derived here

equations.name: Eddy-dissipation model (Magnussen-Hjertager), alternative to β-PDF
equations.expression: R_F = A ρ (ε/k) min( Y_F, Y_O2/s, B Y_P/(1+s) ), A = 4.0, B = 0.5 ; optional 2-step: F + O2 → CO + H2O, CO + ½O2 → CO2, each min(EDM, Arrhenius)
equations.variables: k, ε turbulence; Y mass fractions; s stoichiometric ratio
equations.validity: Turbulent, mixing-controlled flames. Overpredicts T near the burner; CO burnout needs the 2-step version. Constants are the standard published values (Magnussen & Hjertager 1977), not re-verified in this session.
equations.source: Magnussen & Hjertager (1977) Proc. Combust. Inst. 16:719; ANSYS Fluent Theory Guide §7.1.2

equations.name: Shell temperature and through-wall drop
equations.expression: T_shell,in = T_bed + q''/k_mw ; ΔT_wall = q'' δ_s / k_s
equations.variables: q'' shell flux (10-20 kW/m2); k_mw 22-55 W/m2K (Suzuki); δ_s 16-20 mm; k_s 38 (carbon steel) or 19 (310S) W/mK
equations.validity: Lumped per circumferential sector. Hot spot under a burner: use the local q'' from the furnace model
equations.source: Suzuki et al. 2008 (k_mw); derived

sweep:furnace.notes:
BUILT ON PRIOR WORK, NOT REDONE. Reused verified items: Suzuki jacketed kiln data, Hamm energy balance, Sihai/Doing burner and drum specs, Gamboa self-sufficiency, Islam fuel switch, Pohl high-temperature gas, k_m-w with lifters, and the shell penetration and isothermal-shell findings (brief §3.4). New this thread: NCG composition and heating-value bounds (Calero TC, Buah TC, Honus abstract), Beston fuel-per-tonne and start-up sequence (vendor full page), verified Smith WSGG coefficients, Cantera-derived design gas properties and T_ad, and a derived furnace heat-path analysis (scripts in scratchpad/r4calc/gas.py and ht.py).

WHAT COULD NOT BE READ (use as gaps, not targets):
(a) A full vol% table (H2/CH4/C2H4/C2H6/C3H6/C3H8/C4/CO/CO2) for MIXED municipal plastics at 500 °C. López et al. 2010 (Waste Manag. 30:620) and 2011 (CEJ 173:62) are closed, the Tecnalia DSpace has no file, and PMC (Bhatt 2026 rotary kiln) is now behind a reCAPTCHA, which I did not bypass. The design compositions A and B are therefore [H], bracketed by Calero (CH4-dominant, 41-68 MJ/m3 HHV), Honus (81-87 MJ/Nm3 for PE/PP) and Buah (18 MJ/m3 for organics-rich MSW). Run a sensitivity on LHV 35-80 MJ/Nm3.
(b) No source gives measured flue temperatures at inlet or outlet or chimney temperatures for a batch rotary drum. The only measured jacket data is Suzuki (700-800 °C heating gas). The 600-750 °C exit is derived from the shell temperature.
(c) The GB/T 150.2 allowable-stress values for Q245R/Q345R at 400-500 °C were not obtained. Only supplier-stated limits (425/475 °C) are available, and they are secondary.
(d) The EDM constants (A = 4, B = 0.5) and the Churchill-Bernstein and Gnielinski correlations are standard textbook values and were not re-read this session.
(e) No marine-litter-specific NCG data was found. The Venice Lagoon study (>100 kg of real marine litter, about 45 wt% product, about 50 % v/v marine gas oil) and the MARLESS benchmark give no gas composition in the snippets.

MODELLING RECOMMENDATIONS FOR kilnkit/flarekit:
1. Furnace reduced model (runs every batch step): a 3-zone Hottel-type model (fire box under the drum → two side annuli → exit duct) with one refractory node per zone, WSGG gas emissivity (Smith Pw/Pc = 1), refractory→shell gray exchange, and a convection correlation (minor). Fuel: auxiliary diesel or LPG for the first 2-3 h, then NCG from the bed model's gas source term, with excess NCG sent to the flare. Control: a PI controller on bed T at 500 °C sets the firing rate; cap firing at 1.047 MW. Outputs for the live plot: firing rate split by fuel, shell T max and min (hot spot under the burners), and flue T out.
2. 3D LES of the fire box (showpiece, optional): reuse the flare LES. Mixture fraction plus β-PDF equilibrium tables from Cantera, built for 3-4 fuel compositions (diesel vapour or LPG; early CO/CO2-rich NCG, case B; late hydrocarbon NCG, case A) and blended by a fuel index. Use P1/DOM with WSGG plus soot (the existing flare soot model; soot matters only near the burner at λ about 1-1.2). The drum shell is a rotating isothermal-ish cylinder whose T comes from the bed model; return the q''(θ, z) map to the bed model (Picard coupling as in the brief §4.3). Z_st = 0.06-0.09 needs fine resolution near the burner, so a T4 run is feasible on a coarse grid of the fire box only.
3. Validation targets: shell flux 11-16.5 kW/m2 at a 555-630 °C wall (Suzuki); firing efficiency 45-65 % [D]; gross fuel 2.1-2.9 GJ per tonne of feed (vendor); self-sufficiency once NCG flows (30-50 % of the gas, Gamboa); shell T ≈ T_bed + q/k_mw with k_mw 22-55 W/m2K. The shell must be flagged above about 600-650 °C [H] given the Q245R/Q345R limits.
4. Physics message for the event: convection in the jacket is negligible (Re about 2400). The drum is heated almost entirely by radiation from the flame-heated refractory and the CO2/H2O flue, so burner placement creates hot spots. That is where lifters and rotation earn their keep: they renew the wetted wall under the hot spot every revolution and keep the shell close to T_bed + q/k_mw.

Sources searched this thread (beyond the files): eprints.whiterose.ac.uk (Buah), digibug.ugr.es (Calero), arXiv 2411.18467 (WSGG), Semantic Scholar API (Honus, López), chinesestandard.net / goldsupplier (GB150 and steel limits), afs.enea.it Fluent 12 Theory Guide (WSGG form; the EDM node returned 403), Beston/Doing pages saved by thread R1, and the Ma & Zhong Columbia report (r1dl/mazhong.pdf). Note: the source field of the WSGG coefficient finding has a stray 'Johnson/Ladommatos? No:' fragment. The correct attribution is the 7th US National Combustion Meeting paper OT08, reproduced as arXiv 2411.18467, with the original being Smith, Shen, Friedman 1982.

findings.parameter: Commercial batch rotary tyre reactor (Pairan Pyrolysis, Perundurai, Tamil Nadu): geometry and operation
findings.value: Horizontal airtight drum 2.6 m dia × 7.5 m with an internal spiral. Rated 14 t tyres per batch, restricted to 12 t by consent; 10 t loaded on the inspection day. Rotated 0.5-2 rpm during the process. Heated to '300-400 C' by burners firing pyrolysis-oil emulsion (70 % oil / 30 % water condensate), then switched to uncondensed gas. Excess gas burned in a separate firing chamber, then scrubber and a 30 m stack with flare. Plant statement of the cycle: loading 4 h, process 8-10 h, cooling 8-10 h, unloading 4 h
findings.context: Indian CPCB inspection of an 'advanced batch automated' tyre plant (the Doing/Beston drum class) on 06-01-2021

findings.parameter: Suzuki 2008 batch rotary kiln (externally flue-gas heated): transient bed and wall behaviour
findings.value: Cylinder SUS310S, ID 1 m × 1.5 m, 25 mm wall, heating-gas jacket gap 34 mm. Heating gas held at 800 C, then 700 C once the cylinder reached 600 C. Waste was fed only after the jacket exit temperature stabilised (hot start). Inner wall fell by 60 C on feeding. Waste and gas reached true readings 6 min after feeding. Waste reached 460 C 30 min after feeding. Wall-to-waste ΔT just after feeding: 450 K (555 C case) and 520 K (630 C case). ΔT across the wall reached zero at 40 min (630 C case), marking the end of endothermic pyrolysis. Peak flux 11 and 16.5 kW/m². Gas production showed 3 peaks: moisture; grain/paper/wood at 200-380 C; PE/PP/PS. Waste T measured 90 mm from the wall (60 and 90 mm differed by less than 10 C; final char bed about 110 mm); three axial measuring sections; slip ring
findings.context: Simulated MSW of 30 % paper, 25 % wood, 15 % PE, 15 % PP, 5 % PS, 10 % grain (dry basis) plus 10 % moisture. This is the closest analogue to marine litter (plastics, organics, water) with measured transients
findings.source: Suzuki T., Okazaki T., Yamamoto K., Nakata H., Fujita O. (2008) J. Thermal Sci. Technol. 3(3):523-531, §2.2, §3.2-3.4, Figs. 4, 6-7, 9
findings.evidence: 'The heating gas temperature was first maintained at 800 °C ... set to 700 °C when the inner cylinder temperature reached 600 °C'; 'Immediately after the wastes were fed in, the temperature of both surfaces of the inner cylinder fell by 60 °C'; 'the waste temperature rose to 460 °C 30 min after being fed in'; 'The temperature difference became zero 40 min after wastes were fed in'

findings.parameter: Suzuki 2008 Part II: effect of lifters and rotation speed on batch pyrolysis time
findings.value: Pyrolysis time (end of gas production): case 1 (555 C, 2.7 rpm, no lifters) 42 min; case 2 (630 C) 30 min. Six lifters, height 50→200 mm: 40→33 min. 100 mm lifters, number 0/3/6: 42/37/35 min. Rotation 2.7→4.3 rpm (text; the case table lists 4.0 rpm): 42→38 min. Six 200 mm lifters at 4.0 rpm: 31 min, almost the same as raising the wall by 75 K. Mean k_m-w: 38.6 (no lifters) → 45.3 (6 × 200 mm) → 50.1 W/m²K (6 × 200 mm + 4.0 rpm). Lifter height mattered most in the water-evaporation phase, lifter number in the plastic-pyrolysis phase. A 10 % gain in k_m-w needs H_l/H_w > 0.45 or a lifter spacing ratio L_l/L_w < 1. Lifters: 25 mm thick boards, 1500 mm long, spot-welded
findings.context: The only full-text batch dataset that isolates lifters and rpm on heating and pyrolysis time with mixed waste. Their scale-up case: kiln 20 m, 3 rpm, 70 kg/min, bulk density 150 kg/m³, repose 40°
findings.source: Suzuki T. et al. (2008) J. Thermal Sci. Technol. 3(3):532-539, §2.3-2.4, §3.1-3.2, Fig. 2-3
findings.evidence: 'The time required for pyrolysis was 42 min in case No. 1, but only 30 min in case No. 2'; 'Increasing the height of the lifters from 50 to 200 mm reduced the time for pyrolysis from 40 to 33 min'; 'shortened from 42 to 37 min by installing three lifters and ... 35 min with six'; 'Increasing rotating speed from 2.7 to 4.3 rpm reduced the time for pyrolysis from 42 to 38 min'; 'case No. 8 ... pyrolysis time was shortened to 31 min'

findings.parameter: Chinese batch plants (Doing, Kingtiger, Huayin): staged temperatures as reported
findings.value: Light oil gas released at 100 C; liquid oil at 120 C; top output 250-280 C; maximum reaction temperature about 350 C (Kingtiger). sweep:batch.notes:
WHAT THIS ADDS TO THE BRIEF (Case B → IVIG batch drum)
1. A measured industrial batch cycle now exists (CPCB/Pairan, full text). The brief had only vendor cycle claims. Two independent plants agree on the firing sequence: auxiliary oil for ~3-3.5 h, then recycled pyro-gas for ~5 h (Pairan, Bangladesh). The vendor threshold for gas self-sufficiency is 220-280 C on the vapour thermometer (Ma & Zhong).
2. Probe definition is the main validation trap. Every industrial log found (Pairan max 300 C; SK gas separator 255-385 C; vendor '100 C first oil, 250-280 C peak, 350 C max') is a VAPOUR-OUTLET / gas-separator temperature. These are far below the bed and wall temperatures that crack PE/PP (430-500 C) or tyres (400-500 C). The kilnkit model must output T_vapour_outlet(t), T_bed(t), T_shell(t) and T_flue(t) separately, and compare only T_vapour_outlet with these logs. The IVIG '500 graus' is most likely a furnace or shell set-point, not the bed temperature (unverified; ask the IVIG operator which thermocouple it is). Suzuki is the only dataset with bed (90 mm from the wall) and wall temperatures over time.
3. Expected shape of the live plot, consistent across sources: (a) a moisture plateau near 100 C (SK step 1 holds 50 min; Suzuki's first gas peak is moisture). Wet marine litter makes this longer. (b) A cellulosics and light-volatiles stage at 200-380 C (Suzuki peak 2; for marine litter, organics, paper and wood). (c) A main plastic-oil stage while the vapour reading sits at 250-300 C (Pairan 19:00-22:40; SK 255 C plateau). (d) A final rise to 350-385 C as the charge depletes. (e) Fall-off when gas production stops, the end criterion in Suzuki and in vendor practice. A cumulative oil curve should therefore be sigmoidal, with ~3-4 h of lag in a multi-tonne drum (Pairan 4200 L in 8.67 h, mean 485 L/h).
4. Lifters and rpm (Suzuki, full text). They shorten batch pyrolysis by 7-26 % (42→31 min) and raise mean k by 17-30 %. Height matters in the drying phase, number in the plastic phase. The same 26 % gain was obtained by raising the wall from 555 to 630 C. A lab tyre kiln (Syamsiro, secondary) and the brief's [82] show lifters shifting yield toward gas. DEM and contact studies (Zhang 2022, QUST, Ma 2025) agree that the gain from rpm is modest above ~2 rpm. Commercial batch drums run at only 0.4-2 rpm (Pairan 0.5-2; Doing 0.4-0.8).
5. Scale check for the IVIG claim of 6-8 h. Multi-tonne drums need 8-10 h of process (Pairan 8.7 h for 10 t; Bangladesh 8 h for 4.5 t; SK 10.4-12.6 h for 4.5 t plastic; Huayin ~20 h of cycle for 10 t plastic). 6-8 h therefore suggests a smaller charge (≲ 1-3 t; my inference) or a hot start. The '70 % oil' claim exceeds the open data for mixed or real waste plastics in rotary and batch units (40-52 %). Only clean HDPE in semi-batch reaches 89 % liquid (Pires, brief). For wet marine litter with sand and salt, present 70 % as the IVIG claim and report the model's own split with this spread.
6. Recommended transient validation ladder for the batch driver:
   - N2-T1: Suzuki case 1/2/8 — bed T(t) (460 C at 30 min), wall dip of 60 C, k_m-w(t) 22→55, pyrolysis time 42/30/31 min ±20 %, three gas-rate peaks in the right order.
   - N2-T2: Pairan cycle — vapour-outlet T(t) envelope (±30 C after digitising the log), firing switch at 3-4 h, process 8-10 h, cooling to < 50 C in 8-13 h, product split oil 38-45 / char 35 / gas 7-10 % (tyre kinetics needed; otherwise only the time scales).
   - N2-T3: SK Fig. 3 — plastic-batch vapour T(t) for the 1 C/min conventional schedule (~280 C at 240 min, ~345 C at 500 min) and the stepwise 100/255 C plateaus. Burner sequencing: 3 axial zones, inlet to outlet.
   - N2-T4: fuel and duty — ~1.3 MJ of auxiliary fuel per kg feed at 10 t scale, ~1 MW burner, gas surplus to flare after the switch (Gamboa: 30-50 % of the gas covers tyre demand).
7. Not found or not readable (do not use as targets):
   - Liu/Dai/Li 2026 numbers (still unverified).
   - Zhang 2020 FPT 106455 full text (VU repository has no file).
   - The LSBU Northern Cyprus plant paper (server TLS chain error, not bypassed; only 45.6 % oil at 500 C from the summary).
   - Syamsiro full text (TLS error).
   - B-20 vendor page (DNS failure; numbers come from the search summary).
   - Google Patents (blocked; the USPTO PDF was used instead).
   - Islam 2013 full text.
   - Martínez 2013 and Williams 2013 reviews (not reached within the call budget).
   - No IVIG reactor dimensions, charge mass or temperature logs are public; the facility blog has none.
8. Spreads to carry:
   - Bangladesh pressure: +0.03 bar vs 'slight vacuum'.
   - Suzuki rpm: 4.0 (table) vs 4.3 (text).
   - SK hold: 120 min (text) vs 4 h (figure legend).
   - Pairan: the early '1 bar' pressure entries are suspect, and the oil calorific value of 6347 kcal/kg is low (emulsion?).

9. The base-case split table in k.py is inconsistent with the notes' scheme.
10. Salt Cl is about 0.41 wt% dry, not 0.45, because sea salt Cl ≈ 55% of salinity.

findings.value: Mixed waste collected from Guanabara Bay. Temperature '500 graus'. Oil 'na faixa de 70%'. Gas 'extremamente rico', with good calorific value. 'A partir do momento que o reator é carregado, esse processo leva de 6 a 8 horas'. Products: a dark, thick oil 'semelhante ao petróleo', char ('carvão') and gas
findings.context: These are the targets the batch simulation must reproduce: the time to the end of oil production (6–8 h), the oil fraction (~70 %), and a process temperature of 500 °C. These are oral claims, not measurements

findings.parameter: GPU DEM throughput, Blaze-DEM (Govender et al.), linear spring-dashpot spheres, mill with lifters
findings.value: 4 million particles at dt = 2e-5 s took 1.16 h per simulated second (12 FPS) on a GTX 880 laptop GPU, i.e. 4.8e7 particle-steps/s [D]. 10 million particles: 18.5 h per revolution (6 s) on a Kepler GPU, i.e. 4.5e7 particle-steps/s [D]. A 4-million-ball plant mill took 7 h per revolution. Scaling with N is linear. Typical overlap limit δmax ≤ 0.05 r; Δt_max = 1.65e-5 s at 0.025 r in their 2D mill case. Power split at plant scale: 47 % particle-particle, 44 % particle-lifter, 9 % particle-shell
findings.context: Optimized CUDA code, a linear spring-dashpot normal force (Eq. 1) and a Coulomb-limited tangential spring. This is the best open benchmark of 'CUDA-class' DEM on a consumer-class GPU. The T4 has 320 GB/s of bandwidth, the same order as the GTX 880M, so ~5e7 particle-steps/s is an upper target for hand-written kernels on a T4
findings.source: Govender N., Rajamani R.K., Kok S., Wilke D.N. (2015) 'Discrete element simulation of mill charge in 3D using the BLAZE-DEM GPU framework', Minerals Engineering (CSIR preprint)
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'four million particles takes 1.16 hours to simulate one second (12 FPS) on a GTX 880 laptop GPU'; p.18: 'one revolution (6 seconds) using a time-step of 2 × 10−5 ... 7 hours'; '10 million particles ... 18.5 hours'; 'δmax ≤ 0.05r'

findings.value: On 2× A100, one million steps per million component spheres took 0.546 h (single spheres), 0.313 h (3-sphere clumps) and 0.264 h (6-sphere clumps), with linear scaling up to 150 million spheres. Rotating-drum validation (D 0.19 m, 3.6 rpm, plastic and wood spheres or 5-sphere 'cylinder' clumps) on one A5000: 5 s simulated took ~0.20 h for spheres and ~0.60 h for clumps (3× cost)

It replaces the earlier brief estimate of 5.7e6, which came from the Chrono::GPU 'well under 1 h' upper bound and is therefore a floor, not a typical rate. Non-spherical waste pieces modelled as clumps cost ~3× per element

findings.parameter: DEM contact-conduction models and soft-particle corrections (exact forms)
findings.value: Batchelor–O'Brien direct conduction: Q = 4 k_eff a ΔT, with a the contact radius. Zhou–Yu–Zulli correction for softened Hertz contacts: a' = (E/E0)^(1/5) a. Morris–Pannala–Ma–Hrenya (AIChE J 62:4526, 2016): a' = (F_n R_eff/E_eff,0)^(1/3) · (t_c0/t_c)^(2/3), correcting both area and contact duration. Lu–Morris–Li–Benyahia (IJHMT 111:723, 2017), as implemented in DEMLab: a' = (K_n a/K_n0)^(2/3) with K_n0 = (4/3)√R_eff E_eff,0 (dimensionally odd as printed; check the original). Indirect: surrounding-layer particle-fluid-particle model (Rong & Horio 1999; Musser 2011; Morris et al. 2015 IJHMT 89:1277)
findings.context: Needed only if DEM carries heat. The brief's DEM keeps a reduced stiffness (1.5 % overlap), so without correction the contact conduction is exaggerated. For plastics (k ≈ 0.2–0.5 W/mK) the gas-gap (PFP) path dominates (Shi & McCarthy 2005, already in JSON)
findings.source: DEMLab documentation (R.L. Rangel, CIMNE), classes ConductionDirect_BOB, AreaCorrect_ZYZ, AreaCorrect_MPMH, AreaCorrect_LMLB, ConductionIndirect_SurrLayer
findings.evidence: BOB code: 'total_hrate = 4 * eff_conduct * contact_radius * (T2-T1)'; ZYZ: 'R_c' = (E_eff/E_eff,0)^{1/5} R_c'; MPMH: 'R_c' = (F_n R_eff/E_eff,0)^{1/3}(t_c,0/t_c)^{2/3}'

findings.parameter: Coarse-grained (parcel) heat-transfer scaling laws
findings.value: For parcels of ratio k = d_CGP/d_p at equal density (m_CGP = k³ m_p): convection Q_conv,CGP = k³ Q_conv. Particle-particle conduction Q'_pp = k^(3/4) √(f(e_p)/f(e_CGP)) Q_pp,CGP, with e_CGP = √(1 + k(e_p² − 1)), ζ = −ln e/√(π² + (ln e)²) and f(e) = exp[−ζ/√(1−ζ²) · arccos ζ] (exponent reconstructed from PDF text). Particle-fluid-particle Q'_pfp = k² Q_pfp,CGP. Particle-wall Q'_pw = k^(3/4) √(f(e_p)/f(e_CGP)) Q_pw,CGP and Q'_pfw = k² Q_pfw,CGP. The base contact law is Q_pp = 4 R_c λ_e ΔT (Eq. 63)
findings.context: Derived by Lu et al. 2017 and used in a GPU coarse-grained CFD-DEM-IBM of fluidized-bed iron-ore reduction over minutes to tens of minutes of process time. It is the published route if DEM parcels carry heat. For 60–90 mm waste parcels the ratio k is undefined (no single real particle size), so parcels should NOT carry the bed heat transfer in our model
findings.source: Direct reduction of iron ore with hydrogen in fluidized beds: a coarse-grained CFD-DEM-IBM study, arXiv:2311.03908, Sect. 3.3, Eqs. 63–66 and 93–102 (citing Lu, Morris, Li, Benyahia 2017 IJHMT 111:723–735)
findings.evidence: 'Qconv,CGP = k3 Qconv'; 'QCGP pp′ = k3/4 sqrt(f(ep)/f(eCGP)) QCGP pp'; 'eCGP = sqrt(1 + k(e2p − 1))'; 'QCGP pfp′ = k2 QCGP pfp'

findings.parameter: Recurrence CFD (rCFD): time-scale bridging for recurring granular/multiphase flows
findings.value: A short conventional simulation records the recurring flow structures. Recurrence plots let them be extrapolated far beyond the simulated time, and passive or weakly coupled scalars (heat, species) are then transported on the replayed fields. Heat transfer in a lab fluidized bed: speed-up of about two orders of magnitude over CFD-DEM, with very good accuracy against measurements. Two variants: Eulerian (implicit FV passive transport) and Lagrangian (stochastic tracer SDE)
findings.context: A rotating drum is the ideal case. The bed flow is steady in the lab frame (smooth drum, rolling) or exactly periodic with period 2π/(N_L ω) with lifters, so recurrence is exact rather than statistical. This is the literature backing for 'frozen/phase-locked DEM kinematics + Eulerian heat and chemistry for hours'
findings.source: Lichtenegger T., Pirker S. (2016) 'Recurrence CFD – a novel approach to simulate multiphase flows with strongly separated time scales', arXiv:1606.00586; Lichtenegger T., Peters E.A.J.F., Kuipers J.A.M., Pirker S. (2017) arXiv:1706.05934 (heat transfer in fluidized beds)
findings.evidence: 'we observe speed-up factors of about two orders of magnitude at very good accuracy with regard to recent measurements'; 'Eulerian Model A ... Lagrangian Model B'

findings.parameter: Markov-chain models of drum mixing built from DEM
findings.value: Drum cells are the Markov states and the transition matrix comes from short DEM trajectories. It gives a good estimate of particle mixing in a rotating drum (Doucet et al.). In a tablet-coating drum, a short DEM run trained the matrix used for long-time predictions. Agreement with DEM was good when the transition time equalled the cycle time, and the learning time must be long enough for the matrix to converge (l1-norm). A fluidized-bed Markov model ran ~2 orders of magnitude faster than CFD-DEM, with mean-residence-time differences < 2 %
findings.context: A second, cheaper time-lapse option: x_{n+1} = P x_n + sources, about 1e3 cells, 7 h in seconds on the GPU. Good for sweeps (static vs rotating, rpm, lifters). Use it as a cross-check of the Eulerian slice
findings.source: PARTICLES 2025 abstract (Chachia et al.); AIChE 2013 paper 120g 'A Markov chain model for a tablet coating process'; Preprints 202407.1963 and MDPI Processes 13(3):614 (2025)
findings.evidence: Search summaries of the abstracts: 'good agreement with DEM was obtained when the transition time was the cycle time'; 'difference of the mean particle residence time calculated by the two models is less than 2%'

findings.parameter: DEM heat-transfer scaling in drums (Rutgers/ASU: Emady, Yohannes)
findings.value: The bed heating time τ collapses on τ/τ_c = F(φ) with φ = τ_p/τ_c, giving three regimes (Emady 2016, CES). Yohannes et al. 2016 (Phys. Rev. E 94:042902): the controlling time scales are the single-particle heat-up time and the particle-wall contact time; all simulations collapse onto one relation. Adepu et al. 2021 (Comp. Part. Mech., MFIX-DEM vs EDEM): monodisperse beds transfer heat better than polydisperse ones; rotation speed has minimal impact on conduction; lower rolling friction improves heat transfer
findings.context: Use this as a verification target for the continuum bed: rotation speed has a weak effect on conduction-dominated heating, consistent with Chaudhuri and Zhang 2022 in the JSON. For 80 mm plastic parcels, φ ≫ 1 (τ_p ~ d²/α ≈ 6e4 s vs τ_c ≈ 30 s [D]), i.e. heating is slow and 'granular-convection' limited; but real waste is films and hollow bodies, so the bed must be treated as an effective porous medium
findings.source: AIChE 2016 paper 667b abstract; ASU Pure record; AIChE 2018 paper 101c abstract; search summary of Adepu 2021
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'the time to heat up a single particle to the drum wall temperature and the time of contact between a particle and the drum wall ... all of the simulations can be collapsed into one relationship'

findings.parameter: DERIVED: freeboard gas inside the batch drum (vapour flow, residence, cracking)
findings.value: Hypothetical D 2.2 × 6.0 m drum, F 0.35, free volume 14.8 m³. Charge 2–3 t, 85 % volatiles released over an active window of 3–4 h: mean vapour mass rate 0.12–0.24 kg/s; volume rate 0.07–0.23 m³/s (M_w 60–100 g/mol, 450 °C); mean gas residence 64–212 s (half of that at a 2× peak); axial superficial velocity 3–9 cm/s; outlet pipe velocity 2–13 m/s (DN200/DN150). Rotational Re = ωR²/ν ≈ 5e3 at 0.8 rpm; Gr ≈ 3.6e10 for ΔT = 100 K (turbulent natural convection, so RANS/LES, not laminar). Secondary cracking with the brief's Option B (k_O = 1e16 exp(−300 kJ/mol/RT)): conversion over 150 s is 0.8 % at 500 °C, 13 % at 550 °C, 82 % at 600 °C and ~100 % at ≥ 650 °C
findings.context: In a batch drum the vapour stays for minutes, so oil vs gas is decided by the freeboard and shell temperature, not by rotation. The '70 % oil' claim implies that most vapour stays ≤ ~550 °C, i.e. the shell above the bed must not run far above 600 °C over long stretches. The 3D freeboard earns its place here, and so does the furnace control (firing-rate cap). Gas-phase transport is quasi-steady relative to the batch (τ ~ 1–4 min ≪ 7 h)
findings.source: Derived (this work), scratchpad/r5calc/r5.py; Option B kinetics from brief §3.7 [C, verified]
findings.evidence: Script output: 'M=3000kg active 4h: mdot=0.177kg/s ... tau_mean=141s'; 'OptionB k_O(600C)=0.0113 1/s; conv at 75/150/300 s: 0.571/0.816/0.966'

findings.parameter: Reflux/condensation inside a batch reactor changes the product split
findings.value: Mixed HDPE/LDPE/PP/PS in a lab batch reactor with a reflux section at 150–300 °C. Lowering the reflux temperature from 300 to 150 °C raised the gasoline-range yield from 285 to 446 g/kg of solid waste and also raised the C1–C4 gas yield (more heavies are returned for further scission)
findings.context: In the Beston-type drum the unheated front door (~1 m hatch) and the rear vapour outlet, rotary joint and separator act as partial refluxers. Wax that condenses there drips back onto the hot bed and is re-cracked. The freeboard model needs a wax dew-point check on cold surfaces (Riazi cut in props.py) and a reflux return term to the bed; otherwise the oil/gas split is biased
findings.source: Dobó Z., Mahner D., Kecsmár G., Nagy G. (2020) 'The influence of reflux temperature on the yield of transportation fuels during plastic waste pyrolysis', Materials Science and Engineering (Miskolc) 45(1):77–83
findings.evidence: Search summary of the abstract: '285 g/kg of solid waste at 300 °C reflux and 446 g/kg at 150 °C'; 'lowering the reflux temperature also enhances the pyrolysis gas yield, which contains mostly C1–C4'

findings.parameter: DERIVED: furnace ↔ drum time-scale separation (justifies a quasi-steady flame)
findings.value: Steel shell heat capacity per area ρcδ = 5.2e4 / 6.9e4 / 8.6e4 J/m²K for 12/16/20 mm. Shell time constant τ_w = ρcδ/h_tot = 170–580 s (h_tot 150–300 W/m²K). Rotation period 75–150 s (0.8–0.4 rpm). Adiabatic upper bound of the shell temperature swing as a spot passes the flame: 8 K (30 kW/m² over 1/4 rev at 0.8 rpm), 26 K (60 kW/m², 1/4 rev, 0.5 rpm), 65 K (60 kW/m², 1/2 rev, 0.4 rpm). Flame/flue residence ~seconds [U] ≪ rotation ~1–2 min < shell ~3–10 min ≪ batch ~2.5e4 s
findings.context: The furnace can be solved quasi-steadily for a given firing rate and mean shell temperature. Its wall heat-flux map q_f(x, θ_lab) drives a transient 2D (θ, x) shell that rotates through it. The shell's thermal inertia averages the flame's azimuthal non-uniformity to within ~10–60 K, larger at slow rpm. The static drum (rpm 0) loses this averaging, which is the P4O/Hedlund hazard already in the brief
findings.source: Derived (this work), scratchpad/r5calc/r5.py
findings.evidence: Script output: 'shell 16mm: C=6.91e+04 J/m2K; tau_w(h_tot=150)=461s'; 'flame flux 60kW/m2 over 0.25 rev at 0.5rpm: shell swing ~26 K'

findings.parameter: Eulerian (CFD) vs Lagrangian (DEM) for flighted drums, and lifter DEM evidence
findings.value: DEM resolves individual particles and fall lengths. The Eulerian approach was cheaper and did better when the number of flights changed. Lowering the shear modulus in DEM is valid, mainly at low rotation speed. Baffled-drum DEM: thermal time −4 % (no baffles) vs −18 % (16 baffles) from 3 to 30 rpm (verified as-is in the JSON). Lifter heat-transfer DEM (Xie 2017): citing papers conflict

In marine litter (films, ropes) lifters mostly drag a tangled mat, and once the plastic melts, lifters drag a viscous pool (rimming film)

equations.name: Linear spring-dashpot normal force (DEM)
equations.expression: F_N = (K_n δ) n − C_n (v_R·n) n ; K_n = m_eff (ln²e + π²)/t_contact² ; C_n = 2√(K_n m_eff)·(−ln e)/√(ln²e + π²) ; m_eff = (1/m1 + 1/m2)^−1 ; tangential F_T = −min(μ|F_N|, |K_T ∫v_T dt − C_T v_T|)
equations.variables: δ overlap, e restitution, t_contact contact duration, μ friction
equations.validity: Soft-sphere DEM; keep δmax ≤ 0.05 r (Govender) or ~1.5 % d (tamborkit); dt ≈ t_contact/18–/50
equations.source: Govender et al. 2015, Eq. 1–3

equations.name: Batchelor–O'Brien contact conduction with soft-contact corrections
equations.expression: Q_ij = 4 k_eff a (T_j − T_i) ; ZYZ: a' = (E/E0)^(1/5) a ; MPMH: a' = (F_n R_eff/E_eff,0)^(1/3) (t_c0/t_c)^(2/3)
equations.variables: k_eff effective solid conductivity, a contact radius, E softened and E0 real modulus, t_c softened and t_c0 real contact time
equations.validity: Particle k ≫ gas k; for plastics add the particle-fluid-particle path
equations.source: DEMLab docs (Batchelor & O'Brien 1977; Zhou, Yu, Zulli 2010; Morris et al. 2016)

equations.name: Coarse-grained heat transfer scaling
equations.expression: m_CGP = k³ m_p ; e_CGP = √(1 + k(e_p² − 1)) ; Q_conv' = k³ Q_conv ; Q_pp' = k^(3/4) √(f(e_p)/f(e_CGP)) Q_pp,CGP ; Q_pfp' = k² Q_pfp,CGP ; Q_pw' = k^(3/4) √(f(e_p)/f(e_CGP)) Q_pw,CGP ; ζ = −ln e/√(π² + ln²e)
equations.variables: k = d_CGP/d_p coarse-graining ratio
equations.validity: Parcels of identical real particles (same size, species, T); verified in fluidized beds; not defined for multi-material waste parcels
equations.source: arXiv:2311.03908 Eqs. 93–102 (from Lu et al. 2017 IJHMT 111:723)

equations.name: Capillary + lubrication force for molten-plastic ('sticky') contacts
equations.expression: f_c = −κR (δn<0); −κR exp(−δn/λ) (0≤δn≤d_rupt); 0 (δn>d_rupt); κ = 2πγ cosθ ; d_rupt = (1+θ/2)V_b^(1/3) ; λ = 0.9 r^(−1/2) (V_b/R0)^(1/2) ; f_vis = (3/2)πR²η v_n/(δn + δn0), δn0 = 5e-4 d_min
equations.variables: γ surface tension, θ contact angle, V_b bridge volume, η melt viscosity, R = √(RiRj), R0 harmonic mean radius, r size ratio
equations.validity: Pendular liquid bridges between rigid spheres; for melts use it only as a qualitative stickiness model

equations.name: Overall drum heat-transfer coefficient from a heating curve (DEM ↔ continuum equivalence)
equations.expression: ∫ dT̄_bed/(T_w − T̄_bed) = (ᾱ A/(M c_bed)) t ; penetration: α_bed = (2/√π) √((ρck)_bed)/√(t_th,DEM) ; series 1/α = 1/α_ws + 1/α_bed
equations.variables: A heated (covered) wall area, M bed mass, t_th,DEM thermal-mixing time constant
equations.validity: Agitated or rotating beds; calibrate k_bed ↔ α_pp in the stagnant limit
equations.source: Tsotsas, Kwapinska, Saage 2007, Eqs. 1, 7, 10

equations.name: Phase-locked (recurrence) transport of bed scalars on DEM keyframe kinematics
equations.expression: ∂(φρ_s Y)/∂t + ∇·(φρ_s u_k(x, t mod T_p; s) Y) = ∇·(φρ_s D_g,k ∇Y) + ω̇(Y,T) ; u_k from DEM averaged over phase bins; s = charge-state parameter (remaining solid volume / initial)
equations.variables: T_p = 2π/(N_L ω) lifter period (∞ for a smooth rolling bed, so the field is steady in the lab frame), D_g granular diffusivity from DEM MSD, Y species/enthalpy
equations.validity: Valid while the granular state changes slowly versus T_p (hours vs ~1 min); re-key when s, the melt fraction or the regime changes
equations.source: Concept from rCFD (Lichtenegger & Pirker 2016) applied to the drum (this work)

equations.name: Markov-chain bed model
equations.expression: x_{n+1} = P x_n + Δt·S(x_n, T_n) ; P_ij = N(i→j in Δt)/N(i) from DEM trajectories ; Δt = lifter period (or 1 s)
equations.variables: x cell inventories (mass, enthalpy, species), P column-stochastic transition matrix
equations.validity: Converged P (l1-norm test) with Δt ≈ cycle time; homogeneous chain only within one keyframe state
equations.source: Doucet et al.; AIChE 2013 120g; PARTICLES 2025
